name: Argo CD
summary: GitOps delivery for Kubernetes: a controller in the cluster keeps what’s running identical to the manifests in a Git repository.
intro: Most pipelines push: a CI job runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade` against the cluster. Argo CD pulls instead. It runs inside Kubernetes, and each `Application` resource points it at a Git repository, a revision and a path. Its repo server renders the manifests there (plain YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize or Jsonnet), and its application controller compares them with the live objects in the cluster. Any difference marks the application OutOfSync.

Syncing applies the difference, either when someone clicks Sync or automatically. With automated sync, `prune` deletes objects that were removed from Git and `selfHeal` reverts changes made by hand in the cluster. Git therefore becomes the record of what is deployed, and a rollback is a `git revert`. One Argo CD can manage many clusters, and its web UI shows every resource’s health and sync status. Argo graduated from the CNCF in December 2022.
strengths: CI never needs credentials for the cluster: Argo CD runs inside it and pulls from Git
Drift is visible straight away, and `selfHeal` can undo manual `kubectl edit`s
Works with plain YAML, Helm, Kustomize and Jsonnet, and manages many clusters from one place
A clear web UI with a live resource tree, diffs and sync history, plus SSO and RBAC
limits: Kubernetes only; VMs, serverless functions and cloud resources need another tool such as Terraform
By default it checks Git every 2 to 3 minutes (120 s plus jitter), so deploys lag unless you add a Git webhook
It deploys what Git says; building images and updating tags in Git is still CI’s job
Secrets don’t belong in Git as plain text; its docs recommend an in-cluster tool such as Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator

snippet.title: An Application that keeps a namespace in sync with Git

story: Argo began at Applatix, a startup whose engineers open-sourced Argo Workflows, a Kubernetes-native workflow engine, in 2017. In 2018 Intuit acquired Applatix, and the Argo team moved there; its manager, Hong Wang, went on to build the control plane Intuit used for hundreds of Kubernetes clusters. The team wanted every application’s definitions, configuration and environments to be declarative and version-controlled, with deployments that were automated and auditable.

The Argo team at Intuit, with Jesse Suen leading the design and Alexander Matyushentsev leading development, built Argo CD as a Kubernetes controller that follows the GitOps pattern: a Git repository is the source of truth, and software in the cluster continuously makes reality match it. The first commit landed on GitHub in February 2018 and version 0.1.0 was tagged that March.

Argo, made up of Argo CD, Workflows, Rollouts and Events, joined the CNCF as an incubating project in April 2020 and graduated in December 2022. Its three creators later left Intuit to found Akuity around it. Argo CD 3.0 followed in May 2025, turning settings that many users already chose into the defaults.

choices.choice: A controller inside the cluster that pulls from Git
choices.why: Running as a Kubernetes controller lets Argo CD compare the live state with Git continuously and mark any difference `OutOfSync`, instead of trusting that the last CI push still holds. CI also no longer needs credentials for the cluster.
An `Application` is itself a custom resource, so Argo CD can be configured the same declarative way as everything it deploys, including from Git.
Teams already wrote manifests as plain YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize or Jsonnet. Rendering all of them, plus custom plugins, let Argo CD adopt existing repositories instead of demanding a new format.
